name: Comic book
basis: why: few flat inks, outlines and 'a lattice of dots ... imitates the press'; how: dot radius grows as the tone darkens
note: Period comics used Ben-Day mechanical tints (uniform dots); these dots grow with tone, which is halftone. Manga is filed under mechanical tint.

lumenary.blurb: Flat inked colour, hard outlines and printed dots in the shadows.

facts.bestOn: Faces and action scenes with clear edges

why: Cheap comics were printed with a few flat inks, black outlines and dots, so the inked look is mostly a matter of constraints. Posterising limits the colours, edge detection supplies the pen lines, and a lattice of dots in the shadows imitates the press. Together they turn photographic realism into drawing.
how: Snap brightness to a small number of levels and rescale each pixel’s colour so it keeps its hue at the flat level.
Raise saturation around each pixel’s own grey value.
Blur the picture, find edges, and darken pixels toward black in proportion to edge strength.
In darker but not black tones, lay a lattice of dots on a 45 degree grid.
Darken any pixel that falls inside a dot whose radius grows as the tone gets darker.
history: Comic books took their classic form in the late 1930s, when Superman appeared in Action Comics in 1938. Their four-colour printing could not make smooth gradients, so artists and printers used flat colour and dot patterns instead. Pop artists such as Roy Lichtenstein later enlarged those dots into fine art in the early 1960s.
terms: To reduce a picture to a few flat tones.
A regular pattern of dots whose size changes to show tone.
Drawing the final black lines over a pencil sketch.
paragraphs: Three ideas make a photograph look inked. First, posterisation: brightness is snapped to a small number of levels, and the colour is rescaled so each pixel keeps its hue but takes the flat brightness of its level, giving the large flat areas of printed colour. Saturation is then pushed up around the pixel’s own grey value, which is the “pop” slider.

Second, outlines: the same blur-then-Sobel edge detector as in neon glow, but here the edge strength darkens the pixel toward black, so outlines are inked rather than glowing. Third, Ben-Day dots, the mechanical dot patterns of old printing. In the darker (but not black) tones a lattice of dots is laid on a 45° grid, and a pixel is darkened if it falls inside a dot whose radius grows as the tone gets darker. Rotating coordinates by 45° is just a sum and difference scaled by 1/√2.

equations.note: Posterise to n levels and rescale colour to the new brightness; the 0.06 keeps blacks stable.
Dot lattice at 45° with spacing s; ⌊·⌉ rounds to the nearest integer. Applied for tones 0.02 < q < 0.62; dots darken colour to 50%.
Ink: edge strength darkens toward black.
